title: Short Stuff: That's A Head Scratcher
summary: Short Stuff installment on why people scratch their heads when thinking or puzzled. The hosts go through several explanations: a vestigial remnant of an aggressive arm-raising reflex when angry, self-soothing through touch (citing former FBI counterintelligence agent Joe Navarro's 2009 Psychology Today article and a 2017 Scientific Reports study of rhesus macaques, where stressed monkeys that scratched were attacked less), displacement activity (animals and people redirecting stress into unrelated behavior), and a dominant learning mode explanation where tactile or visual learners touch their heads or look up. The episode ends with a brief sign-off and an ad read.

segments.title: Opening banter and setting up head scratching
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the Short Stuff episode and joke about the producer. They frame the topic: scratching your head when thinking is a cultural idiom with no definitive explanation.

segments.title: Evolutionary remnant explanation
segments.summary: One explanation is that head scratching is a remnant of an ancestral anger response, where the arm rises to strike and is stopped, leaving a rubbing of the head or neck. The hosts note it seems thin but link it to rubbing the forehead or neck when furious.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break before returning to the topic.

segments.title: Self-soothing and Joe Navarro
segments.summary: Former FBI counterintelligence agent Joe Navarro, in a 2009 Psychology Today article, said stress prompts hand-to-body touching as self-soothing. The hosts say the head is touched because the brain is there.

segments.title: Rhesus macaque stress study
segments.summary: A 2017 Scientific Reports study found that higher-ranking rhesus macaques that scratched or itched when stressed were left alone by other macaques more than those that did not. The hosts connect this to a Seinfeld bit about looking stressed to avoid people.

segments.title: Displacement activity
segments.summary: Displacement activity is when an animal facing conflicting options performs an unrelated behavior, such as preening or pecking the ground. The hosts give a bike-crash anecdote from Athens as an example of a human doing the same.

segments.title: Learning modes and wrap-up
segments.summary: A final explanation holds that head touching or looking up reflects a dominant learning mode, with tactile and visual learners reverting to their preferred sense. Josh says he is a strong visual learner. The episode closes with a sign-off and an ad read.
